extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students/scholars of literary theory and poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and evaluating poetic diction, word-formation, metaphor, and the construction of unified narrative or dramatic plots (epic, tragedy, iambic, etc.). Emphasis on appropriateness of diction to genre, unity of action, plausibility, and the artistic uses of linguistic license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity (of action or of thing signified)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition or phrase may form a unity in two ways—either as signifying one thing, or as consisting of several parts linked together. (Example: the Iliad is one by the linking together of parts; the definition of man by the unity of the thing signified.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots so they are a 'single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.' Avoid trying to make an epic of an entire vast subject; detach a single portion and admit episodes only insofar as they serve the unity. Episodes may diversify but must not destroy unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of words and word-formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are classified as simple and double (or compound), and may be triple, quadruple, or multiple; a compound word can be composed of significant and non-significant elements or of significant elements joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of how compound and derived forms function in diction; certain forms (compounds, lengthenings, contractions, alterations) give distinction and can be used artistically but must be employed with moderation and propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical kinds (current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, altered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word is either current, or strange, or metaphorical, or ornamental, or newly-coined, or lengthened, or contracted, or altered. Current/proper words are in general use; strange words are current in another country; newly-coined words are invented by the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mixture: current words give perspicuity; strange/ornamental/metaphorical words raise style above the commonplace. Excess of any one class (only current or only strange/metaphorical) leads to defects (meanness, riddle, or jargon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity without meanness (balance of plainness and elevation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style—using only current words—is often mean; a lofty style uses unusual words. The ideal balances perspicuity and distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer current words for clarity but introduce a measured infusion of rare/metaphorical/ornamental elements to avoid banality. Avoid wholly ordinary diction (too mean) and wholly unusual diction (becomes riddle or jargon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor: forms and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference either from genus to species, from species to genus, from species to species, or by analogy/proportion. One may also qualify the metaphor by adding the term to which the proper word is relative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphor to reveal likenesses of things; good metaphors require an 'eye for resemblances' and mark genius. Employ metaphors appropriate to the metre and genre (see matching diction to genre). Overuse produces riddles; improper or forced metaphors are grotesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning diction into a riddle or a jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: A style wholly composed of metaphors is a riddle; wholly of strange words is a jargon. The essence of a riddle is to express true facts under impossible combinations, which is achieved by metaphors; jargon arises from continuous use of rare terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain moderation: introduce metaphors and rare words where they illuminate or elevate, not merely to obtrude cleverness. Obtrusive licenses of speech are grotesque and ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses of speech (lengthening, contraction, alteration) used for distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is lengthened when its vowel is exchanged for a longer one or a syllable is inserted; contracted when part is removed; altered when part is left and part re-cast. Deviations from normal idiom in exceptional cases give distinction while partial conformity gives perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics err in censuring such licenses wholesale. Use them sparingly and appropriately to produce distinction without obscuring meaning. Excessive or obtrusive use is caricatured and destroys effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of diction to genre and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain kinds of words suit particular genres: compound words suit dithyrambs, rare words heroic poetry, metaphors iambic; in heroic poetry many varieties are serviceable; iambic aims to reproduce familiar speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction consistent with the genre and metre: heroic verse tolerates stately diction and rare words; iambic and conversational metres demand more current/proper words and metaphors appropriate to speech. Do not mix metres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and consistency of metre
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic measure is the stateliest and most massive and admits rare words and metaphors; iambic and trochaic tetrameters are stirring measures (trochaic akin to dancing, iambic expressive of action). Mixing metres is incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the metre that fits the scale and character of the poem and keep consistency. For epic-scale narrative, heroic metre is appropriate; other metres suit their traditional functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and scope suited to a single view
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; poems should be of a scale answering to a group of tragedies presented at a single sitting. Do not try to encompass an entire vast theme at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit subject-matter so the whole can be apprehended as a single whole. If the theme is very large, detach a portion and use episodes to enrich without losing manageable unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of narrative imitation on dramatic principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative imitation in single metre should be constructed on dramatic principles: it should have a single action whole and complete, resembling a single coherent picture of a living being to produce pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when narrative, arrange material so it imitates dramatic unity (single plotline) rather than a disconnected sequence of events; aim for coherence similar to a staged action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes and enlargement in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry can present many simultaneous events and admit episodes that, if relevant, add mass and dignity and divert and relieve the story; Homer detaches a single portion and admits episodes to diversify the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include episodes to add grandeur and variety, but ensure they relate to and support the central action and do not fragment unity; episodic material should be relevant and purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited authorial intrusion / focalization through characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; the poet is an imitator. Homer brings in characters at once, each with characteristic qualities; the poet's role is to let actions/voices show character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer presenting character through action and speech rather than long authorial commentary. Excessive authorial presence weakens imitation and reduces dramatic immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and treatment of the wonderful/irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is admissible but the poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities. The tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts; irrationalities should, if possible, be excluded or lie outside the action of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the marvelous only where it serves effect and where plausibility (or the audience's false inferences) can veil absurdity. Do not rely on irrational incidents within the drama unless unavoidable and artistically justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaborated diction reserved for pauses in action
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought; conversely, character and thought are obscured by excessively brilliant diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ornate language in moments of reflection or pause; in moments of character-revealing action or thought, favor clearer, character-appropriate speech so as not to obscure intention or personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding errors that damage the essence vs. tolerating accidental technical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the art of poetry there are two kinds of faults—those which touch its essence, and those which are accidental (technical mistakes in particular arts). An error touching the essence (incompetent imitation) is serious; accidental inaccuracies are less serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure fundamental imitation and composition are correct (structure, unity, character). Minor technical errors (e.g., inaccurate craft details) may be tolerable if they do not impair the poetic effect, though avoidable errors should be avoided when they do not serve an artistic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of rule-violations by artistic ends
rubrics_metrics.description: If the poet represents things impossible according to the rules of his art, the error may be justified if the end of the art (producing the proper effect) is thereby attained; if the end could be attained without violating rules, the violation is not justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depart from technical or conventional rules only when the artistic effect requires it and cannot be achieved otherwise. Favor solutions that achieve effects without unnecessary rule-breaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential structural elements of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy may be simple or complex; its parts (except song and scenery) include Reversals, Recognitions, and Tragic Incidents; thoughts and diction must be artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing tragedy, check for presence and skillful integration of reversals and recognitions, and that thoughts and diction are appropriate to tragic ends. Ensure the parts cohere to produce catharsis and dramatic completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and characteristic delineation of persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters introduced should be 'none of them wanting in characteristic qualities, but each with a character of his own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create or evaluate characters by their distinct, consistent qualities manifest in speech and action. Avoid flat or indistinct personages; each significant figure should be recognizable by traits and choices.
